Sunrise. F.W. Murnau's 1927 American masterpiece depicting the moral and emotional journey of a married couple tempted toward destruction by urban vice and infidelity, then restored to love and grace through near-tragedy. A visual symphony of German Expressionist technique applied to intimate human drama, it won the first Academy Award for Best Picture in 1929 and remains a profound meditation on redemption.

Murnau directed this as his first American film after Nosferatu's success, made for Fox Studios. The Man is tempted by a seductive woman—the Woman from the City—to drown his wife. When they go to the city, its lights and attractions momentarily seduce the Man, but he abandons the plan. After nearly drowning his wife, the Man rescues her, and in the Sunrise they experience rebirth and renewed love.

The film shifts visually from dark German Expressionist shadow in the rural sequences, embodying guilt and temptation, to bright, stylized city scenes conveying artifice and corruption, then back to redemptive nature. Murnau used innovative visual effects: miniatures for city shots, soft focus for romantic moments, and chiaroscuro to embody moral psychology. The title references Psalm one thirteen and the promise of spiritual dawn after moral night.

The Academy recognized Sunrise as an artistic achievement immediately, awarding it the inaugural Outstanding Picture award in nineteen twenty-nine, later renamed Best Picture. The film became Murnau's final major work. He died in a car accident in nineteen thirty-one, casting Sunrise as a tragic culmination. It brought Expressionist language to intimate drama while exploring loneliness and human connection, standing alongside other contemporary masterworks equally beloved but opposite in tone.
